snippet.title: Figma Motion basics: Easing
snippet.description:
Let’s learn about easing in Figma Motion.

Keyframes define what changes and when. Easing defines how it gets there by controlling whether an animation accelerates, decelerates, or both. It's what separates motion that looks correct from motion that feels correct.

Learn more about Figma Motion: https://www.figma.com/blog/introducing-figma-motion/ & https://help.figma.com/hc/en-us/articles/41274629073303

Learn more about motion design principles: https://help.figma.com/hc/en-us/sections/41236726027287-Motion-design-fundamentals-collection

snippet.title: Figma Motion basics: Motion path
snippet.description:
Let’s learn about motion paths in Figma Motion. When you add position keyframes to an animation, that movement is displayed as a motion path on the canvas. Motion paths are made up of dots which indicate an animation’s speed, also known as easing, and boxes, which mark the position of each keyframe.

Learn more about Figma Motion: https://www.figma.com/blog/introducing-figma-motion/ & https://help.figma.com/hc/en-us/articles/41274629073303

Learn more about motion design principles: https://help.figma.com/hc/en-us/sections/41236726027287-Motion-design-fundamentals-collection

snippet.title: Figma Motion basics: Keyframes
snippet.description:
Keyframes are one of two ways to animate objects in Figma Motion. A keyframe marks a point in time where you set a specific value for a layer property. When you set a second keyframe for the same property but with a different value, Figma Motion animates the transition between them.

Learn more about Figma Motion: https://www.figma.com/blog/introducing-figma-motion/ & https://help.figma.com/hc/en-us/articles/41274629073303

Learn more about motion design principles: https://help.figma.com/hc/en-us/sections/41236726027287-Motion-design-fundamentals-collection

snippet.title: Figma Motion basics: Motion timeline
snippet.description:
Let’s learn about the Figma Motion timeline.

To access the timeline, switch the toolbar toggle to Motion. The timeline lives across the bottom of your screen. This is where you’ll set keyframes, adjust animation placement and length, and preview your animations.

Learn more about Figma Motion: https://www.figma.com/blog/introducing-figma-motion/ & https://help.figma.com/hc/en-us/articles/41274629073303

Learn more about motion design principles: https://help.figma.com/hc/en-us/sections/41236726027287-Motion-design-fundamentals-collection

snippet.title: The canvas is not dead ft. Catt Small (Dropbox) | Config 2026
snippet.description:
You've probably heard it: 'the canvas is dead. Just prompt your way to a UI and ship it.' But Catt doesn't work on simple problems. She designs for tens of millions of users, inside products with years of context and use cases AI tools can't easily handle. When the complexity is that deep, you can't skip the part where you actually think. She'll walk through her framework for deciding what deserves deep, by-hand exploration versus what to hand off to the machine. You'll leave knowing how to match your tools to your actual problems.
____________________________________________________

snippet.title: Human methods, new material: AI for the classroom ft. Mubarak Marafa & Wendy Liao | Config 2026
snippet.description:
How do you build with AI for a world as human, messy, and high-stakes as the classroom? This talk takes you inside the 0–1 journey of Goodnotes Classroom: from real teacher workarounds and classroom observations to fast prototypes, co-creation sessions, and product decisions shaped by educators themselves. We’ll share how human methods became the foundation for designing with AI as a new material, and why the best way to build faster may be to get closer to the people you’re building for.

snippet.title: Own the loop: how designers and researchers win with AI evals ft. Setor Zilevu (Figma) | Config 2026
snippet.description:
AI is everywhere, but how do we know if it's actually good? The teams winning with AI aren't just moving fast, they're measuring well. And that measurement starts with a human-centered definition of "good" that lives in design and research. AI evals have long been an engineering problem. That's changing. As capabilities commoditize, design is the new moat. This talk is an invitation for designers and researchers to lead and become architects of how we evaluate AI against real human needs.

snippet.title: Usernames on Instagram: how a craft fix became an identity crisis ft. Rose McManus | Config 2026
snippet.description:
A small craft fix in Instagram's interface spiraled into a much bigger question: What is a username, actually? And what does it mean for how we understand identity online?This talk traces that spiral—from @dril to Baudrillard, from the pumpkin spice latte to the phone icon that still looks like a landline—and arrives somewhere concrete: In the Internet Age, users don't just adapt to what we build, they create something new with it. Representations drift from reality, and people don’t just adapt to products—they complete them. The result is a firsthand case study in product judgment when human behavior becomes the strongest constraint, why designing with curiosity and far-fetched futurism matters even more in fast-moving environments.
____________________________________________________

snippet.title: Design systems anarchy ft. Lauren LoPrete (Mercury) | Config 2026
snippet.description:
Most people don't get into design systems to be a cop. But we've become exactly that. Product teams go around us while we create rules nobody follows. Punk figured this out decades ago. You need shared ethos, basic infrastructure, and people who care. Quality comes from culture, not compliance. Drawing from years running an indie record label and nearly 10 years leading systems at scale at Block, Dropbox, and Expedia, this talk applies punk's blueprint to systems. AI handed designers the means of production. The gatekeeping model is dead. Stop managing systems. Start nurturing subcultures.
____________________________________________________

Introducing a design system at a design-led company can be like trying to whip a tablecloth off a beautifully set table while people are still eating—and maybe put a nicer tablecloth on at the same time. As part of Notion’s newly formed design system team (est. 2025), we’ll share the tools and techniques we’re using to refactor Notion’s visual foundations and improve things from the inside, without slowing down our peers or compromising the spirit of thoughtful, handcrafted care that makes Notion feel like Notion.
____________________________________________________

snippet.title: The future is low-tech: lessons from the early 2000s ft. Jésabel DC | Config 2026
snippet.description:
We’ll rewind to the early 2000s—when tech was low-tech, playful and non-extractive. Think: loading bars, Tamagotchis and RollerCoaster Tycoon in a cereal box. This talk explores calm, nervous-system-friendly design: attention regulation, slowness as a feature, autonomy-first mechanics, real-world interaction and gentle feedback loops. A call for designers and builders to make tech feel human again.

snippet.title: The world of street art and care-filled design ft. Ella Rochelle-Lawton | Config 2026
snippet.description:
After studying art and design at UC Berkeley, Ella Rochelle-Lawton ran off to join the circus and designed a billboard about it. Since then, teaching street art history and spray paint has taught her that the best design lives on the street, where people can touch it and make it their own. In this talk, she'll share how working with teams from Adobe, Google, and Figma transformed her view of design from pixels to people. She’ll explore how street art, from the local legends to international artists, build belonging, redefine public space, and inspire community throughout the design process.
____________________________________________________

snippet.title: Designed to be read: making a system AI can actually use ft. Harvey Whiting (Meta) | Config 2026
snippet.description:
Hear the story of how Meta worked directly with Figma to test design systems in Figma Make. You’ll learn how, in our quest to push the boundaries of AI-driven quality, Meta’s business design system team was inspired to rebuild their legacy design system for business tools from the ground up. Our talk covers the “sloppy” challenges we encountered, how we resolved them in close partnership with Figma, and outlines a 3-step repeatable playbook that any team can use to deliver high-quality AI-generated designs—even without rebuilding your entire design system.

snippet.title: The invisible mechanisms in your interfaces ft. Johannes Mutter (mutter.co) | Config 2026
snippet.description:
For 15 years, Johannes has been taking interfaces apart and collecting the mechanisms underneath. There’s a name for when your cursor sits between bold and regular and the system can’t tell you which wins. It’s called cursor affinity. Your tools are full of mechanisms like this — each with an inventor, a constraint, and a lineage you can trace. This talk takes them apart, names them, and hands you a practice for disassembling any interface you touch. You’ll leave with the words to make others see what you see.
____________________________________________________

snippet.title: Design for the future of apps ft. Craig Labenz (Google) | Config 2026
snippet.description:
Generative AI is not only about text chats and image generation. At Google, AI is also increasingly used to compose ephemeral UI on demand, a pattern called Generative UI. While this promises unparalleled personalization for each user, it also risks regressions in UX pillars like consistency and clear information hierarchy. Learn how designers can adapt design systems to realize the full potential GenUI while also mitigating its risks.

snippet.title: Legibility by design ft. Ryan Powell (Waymo) | Config 2026
snippet.description:
Building trust in AI isn't about transparency; it’s about communication design. Whether it’s an autonomous vehicle or a generative agent, the challenge is the same: how much should a system communicate? Drawing from years at Waymo, this session explores a framework for trust. We’ll move beyond automation toward legibility, where users understand intent rather than just monitoring tasks. Learn to calibrate feedback to avoid alert fatigue and build AI products that feel predictable and fundamentally trustworthy.

snippet.title: Designing with confidence in an AI-powered world ft. Bobby Meixner (UserTesting) | Config 2026
snippet.description:
AI has fundamentally changed the pace of design. Ideas move faster. Iterations are instant. Options are endless. But speed introduces a new tension: decisions that are harder to defend. In this session, Bobby Meixner shares findings from UserTesting’s latest research on defensible design in the age of AI and explores how leading teams are closing the confidence gap. You’ll see how embedding real human insight directly inside the design workflow allows teams to move quickly, without sacrificing certainty. Because in an AI-powered world, the real advantage isn’t speed. It’s conviction.
____________________________________________________

snippet.description:
Want to animate like the pros and spend less time wrestling the graph editor? This session reveals a capture-to-curve workflow that turns recorded gestures into clean, editable timing you can drop into the tools you use. We will map a motion in the room to a UI element live and unpack a practical loop: capture, curve, polish, name. You will leave with a shared motion language you can reuse across design and code, plus techniques to make interfaces feel natural so newcomers move with confidence and experts move faster. We will demystify the curve editor and show how to ship feel, not graphs.

snippet.title: The rules are the art: creating with AI ft. Holly Herndon | Config 2026
snippet.description:
Holly Herndon has spent the last decade building at the frontier of music and AI, from the albums Platform and PROTO to Holly+, the first artist-controlled voice model, to the data consent tools behind Spawning. This talk covers her approach to making art with AI, what she calls Protocol Art: a process-based practice of designing the rule set that creates the conditions for art to be made. Holly will discuss how the model-making process becomes a site of authorship, and where her studio with Mat Dryhurst is heading next: orchestrating agents while remaining at the conceptual center.

snippet.title: Connecting Figma and Weave
snippet.description:
At Figma, we believe the best work always happens in the open—on the canvas, where the process becomes not just visible, but shared. Our acquisition of Weavy, now Figma Weave, last year was the first step in bringing design and creative production closer together in the same collaborative space. With Weave's node-based workflows, the process of making and editing imagery, video, audio, and 3D becomes a sequence you and your teammates can inspect, tweak, and repeat. 

Today, we're bringing Weave tools onto the Figma canvas and Weave workflows to the Figma Community—and with the Figma node in Weave soon to come, you’ll do less translating between design and creative production, and more fine-tuning of your vision.

Learn More Here → https://www.figma.com/blog/connecting-figma-and-weave/

snippet.title: Introducing Figma Motion: Your canvas now has a timeline
snippet.description:
Motion now lives on the canvas—in the same file as your components, your variables, and your team—so your designs can come to life from day one.

When it’s done right, motion is one of the most expressive elements in a design. It shapes how users read hierarchy and feel the thought behind an interaction. A creative decision this impactful should be scoped and shaped from the start, with input from the whole team. 

Starting today, motion is native to the same canvas where the rest of your designs live. Motion is no longer a bottleneck or a one-person job. Any designer can now prompt the Figma agent to build motion directly on the new animation timeline, lowering the barrier to creation while raising the ceiling of what's possible. And with Dev Mode access and functionality, the whole experience is built for a much smoother handoff.

Learn more → https://www.figma.com/blog/introducing-figma-motion/

snippet.title: Shader effects and fills, now in Figma
snippet.description:
Figma agent can now also build shaders—small, customizable programs powered by WebGPU that define how pixels render. Think dither, liquid metal, fractal noise. They come in two flavors:

→ Shader effects are like native Figma effects, but built entirely by you—like particle stretch, lens distortion, color outline, and more. You can stack them, adjust the properties, and couple them with native effects for the result you want.

→ Shader fills are dynamic and generative—going far beyond solid colors and gradients, including watercolor, moiré, pattern grids, and more.

Learn more → https://www.figma.com/blog/agent-custom-tools-context-skills/

snippet.title: Getting Started with Custom Skills | ft. Amy Lima & TJ Pitre
snippet.description:
Learn how to use custom skills with Figma's native MCP to streamline your design workflows.

Designer advocate Amy Lima and design systems veteran TJ Pitre (creator of the Figma Console MCP) walk you through the definition, anatomy, and refinement of a custom skill so you can work smarter with AI on the canvas. This skill brings working code prototypes into structured Figma design files, exploding each interaction flow into separate frames, using your design system components, and annotating interaction details natively in Figma → https://github.com/alima-max/prototype-to-figma-skill/tree/main

TJ Pitre recently joined our team at Figma as a product architect for Design Systems, working across groups on our DS offering. TJ doesn't think about design systems in the abstract — he's been in the weeds building them, teaching them, and rethinking what they need to be now. His expertise maps directly to our product priorities: making agents good at using design systems inside and outside of Figma, while continuing his work at Southleft's as its founder and CEO.

More from Amy's interview with TJ →  https://youtu.be/zrDt4T_SLgE

snippet.description:

→ Automatic positioning: Content automatically shifts to fill gaps when items are deleted.
→ Automatic rows: Rows are automatically created or removed as you add or delete content.

snippet.title: Create flexible components with Slots | Figma
snippet.description:
Add flexibility to your design system with Slots! Slots are customizable containers within components that let you add, modify, and organize assets directly inside an instance. Let’s take a look at how Slots can transform your design workflow…so you can say “goodbye” to rigid design systems and “hello” to components that bend without breaking!

Feel free to duplicate the Figma playground file to play around with Slots → https://www.figma.com/community/file/1610367877471727305

Check out the Figma Help Center article to learn more about Slots → https://help.figma.com/hc/articles/38231200344599/

snippet.title: Getting started with Slots | Figma
snippet.description:
Learn how Slots unlock dynamic components instances — from adding another menu option, button, or even an icon to your instances, without detaching.

Slots are great for:

• Components with repeating elements, like task lists or tabs.
• Components that are frequently customized, like cards or modals.
• Simplifying bloated design systems by decreasing variants or hidden layers.
• Reducing detaches so instances continue receiving updates from the main component.

Rolling out now in open beta over the next week. Available to everyone on a full-seat.

Playground file → https://www.figma.com/community/file/1610367877471727305/figma-slots-playground

Learn more here → https://help.figma.com/hc/articles/38231200344599/

snippet.title: Understanding Today’s Design Job Market (Figma’s New Study + Daniel Wert)
snippet.description:
In this episode of FigBrew, Andrew Hogan speaks with Daniel Wert, CEO of Wert & Co., about our new study on hiring in design — and what it reveals about the current moment in the market.

Together, they unpack the rebound in design hiring, the surge in demand for senior ICs, and the state of junior hiring. Daniel shares what he’s seeing firsthand from running design leadership searches across industries — and where companies may be thinking too short-term.

From the quest for a “founding designer unicorn” to the Moneyball approach to building teams, this conversation reframes how design talent should be evaluated, developed, and structured for the current environment.

They also explore what AI literacy really signals to employers, why mentorship and player development matter more than ever, and what candidates should be doing differently right now.

You’ll learn:
 • What our new hiring study reveals about the design market
 • Differences between hiring in 2024, 2025, and today's environment
 • What “leadership” in design really means (beyond titles)
 • Why the founding designer role is often misunderstood
 • The danger of hiring only senior ICs
 • Why most startups should think like Moneyball, not the Yankees
 • How flattening orgs hurt mentorship and long-term development
 • Why experience diversity matters as much as other forms of diversity
 • What candidates should actually be doing to stand out
 • How to build AI case studies if your company hasn’t adopted AI yet

00:00 Intro and our new hiring study
 00:05:30 Founding designers and the versatility trap
 00:10:51 Unicorn hiring and the Moneyball alternative
 00:20:44 Flattened orgs, mentorship, and senior IC demand
 00:24:59 The long-term risk of under-hiring junior talent
 00:30:42 What candidates should be doing right now
 00:40:12 The future of design: brand, storytelling, and industrial resurgence

snippet.title: In the file: Building Modern Product Workflows in the Age of AI, with Botim | Figma
snippet.description:
Join Sherizan and Nayanika from Botim for an inside look at how their team designs, builds, and scales product experiences using Figma. In this “In the File” livestream, they share how they structure files, manage components and variables, and collaborate across design and engineering to ship consistently at scale.

They walk through real examples from their workflow, unpack decisions behind their design system, and discuss how they balance speed, quality, and cross-team alignment. Expect practical tips on maintaining scalable libraries, improving handoff, and evolving a system as the product grows.

Whether you’re a design system maintainer, a product designer working in complex files, or collaborating closely with engineering, this session offers actionable insights you can apply to your own team.

snippet.title: Why Design, Strategy, and Technology Are Inseparable
snippet.description:
Design strategy spans business intent and execution, but it’s rarely taught or practiced that way.

In this episode of FigBrew, Andrew Hogan sits down with Garkay Wong, author of The Art of Design Strategy, to explore how designers can better articulate the value of their work in an era of rapid technological change. Drawing on her experience across service design, innovation strategy, and consulting, Wong explains why many traditional business frameworks fall short and how design can play a stronger role in strategic decision-making.

The conversation centers on TRACES, Wong’s framework for aligning design work with organizational goals by accounting for technical debt, regulation, audience shifts, competition, economic forces, and substitute technologies. Together, they discuss why alignment matters more than brainstorming, how collaboration between designers and non-designers is evolving, and what it means to make ideas tangible in order to improve decision quality.

They also examine how generative AI is increasing teams’ capacity to create, why prioritization matters more than ever, and why judgment, context, and craft remain essential as production accelerates.

What you’ll learn
• Why designers often struggle to communicate value to the business
• How the TRACES framework helps teams align and make better decisions
• Why technology now sits at the center of strategy conversations
• How collaboration between designers and non-designers is changing
• What generative AI means for capacity, prioritization, and craft

snippet.title: FigBrew: Understanding The Next Era Of Strategy With Tamara Moellenberg
snippet.description:
What if looking at the world the way designers do could unlock a company’s next competitive edge?

In this episode of FigBrew, Andrew Hogan speaks with Tamara Moellenberg, associate partner at ReD Associates, about a strategy framework that goes beyond optimization and user-centricity. Drawing on anthropology, ethnography, and the social sciences, Moellenberg introduces the idea of “worlds” as a third wave of strategy, focused on culture, communities, and shared systems of meaning.

Together, they explore why many classic strategy tools no longer explain outsized success, how companies like Hermès and LEGO build value by tapping into cultural worlds, and why understanding energy, relevance, and social dynamics can matter more than market size alone. The conversation also touches on how generative AI raises the stakes for cultural resonance and what it means for organizations navigating uncertainty.

You’ll learn:
• Why traditional strategy frameworks are no longer enough
• How “worlds” explain cultural advantage and differentiation
• What companies like Hermès and LEGO get right
• How to think about energy, relevance, and the right to win
• Why generative AI makes cultural resonance more important

snippet.title: Benedikt Lehnert on AI’s Real Adoption Curve: Design Is the Diffuser
snippet.description:
Design doesn’t just make tech usable—it makes it adoptable. Benedikt Lehnert is a design executive and Entrepreneurship and Design Fellow, at Princeton University. In this interview he draws on history to walk through his take on AI as Normal Technology and how design will accelerate (or hinder) AI’s diffusion.

We trace the path from steam and electrification to the personal computer and today’s AI systems—showing how design translates human intent into action. And, we discuss lessons from the PC productization, a Bauhaus for AI idea, and what skills (taste, craft, critical thinking) matter most in the age of generative models.

What you’ll learn
- Ben’s thoughts on AI’s diffusion timeline
- How design bridges invention → adoption → diffusion
- The role of productization (e.g., Macintosh) in making tech personal
- Why a “Bauhaus for AI” blends data literacy, ethics, and craft
- Practical skills to differentiate beyond average, AI-generated outputs

00:06:32 Diffusion model & design’s role
00:08:55 Case studies: streamlined trains & Olivetti

00:24:43 Why chat UIs hook us → toward multimodality

snippet.title: 🇯🇵 Get Started with Figma Make
snippet.description:
Figma Makeをこれから始めたい方にぴったりの、わかりやすく実践的な「初級セッション」です。

snippet.title: How teams in India design for diversity and scale with Figma
snippet.description:
When your users span 20+ official languages and countless dialects, alignment isn’t a nice-to-have—it’s the product.

In this video, leaders from Fynd, Meesho, Swiggy, and Times Internet show how they treat design as a business differentiator, and how Figma helps them bring partners into the work early, collaborate in real time, and move from idea to launch faster.

Featuring: Sreeraman MG (Fynd), Leena Jacob (Meesho), Saptarshi Prakash (Swiggy), and Ashish Jaiswal (Times Internet).
